doc.title: Jason Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2025

title: Mark Turner's exercise on listening to the rhythm section
summary: Palmer describes Turner's clinic exercise of playing only in response to the rhythm section.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Do you find that there’s been occasions where you play less, a bit less, because you’re working with such wonderful — a wonderful rhythm section?

Yeah. Yup. Um hum. You know I’ve been playing with a tenor player, Mark Turner — I’ve been in his band for about ten years now, a little over ten years, going on eleven now I think. And we’ve done some clinics together at certain schools and everything. And he did this one exercise that I learned a lot from where he brought a horn player up and there was a rhythm section accompanying. And so they all played a tune. But he told the saxophone player he said, “Okay so when the tune starts I don’t want you to play anything until you hear something from the rhythm section that is worth responding to, or something that you can contribute to based on what they play.” Because a lot of times © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

horn players, they’ll get up and they want to just play their stuff and have other people follow them. Whereas he said, “Okay I want you to listen. Maybe listen to the drummer’s snare. Or maybe listen to the piano player’s left hand, you know what kind of rhythm they’re playing. Or maybe the bass player’s playing a certain harmonic or something you know.” And so I said wow, that’s a really cool way to go in to a solo when you’re improvising, just to say okay I’m going to be influenced by what I hear around me, and only play that.
That takes a lot of discipline.
So you don’t go in playing a lick-based solo. You go in like truly improvising based on what you hear around you. And so that’s a real unique tool to use.
